newsitem.title: UK: FORECAST - EMU seen unmoved by left win in France.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - EMU seen unmoved by left win in France.

text.p: A Socialist win in France's national elections may cause some turbulence but would be unlikely to derail European economic and monetary union (EMU), a Reuters survey showed on Wednesday.

Thirty-three of 49 respondents to the monthly poll of EMU expectations said a victory for Socialist leader Lionel Jospin over the centre-right government of Prime Minister Alain Juppe in the May 25-June 1 elections would have no effect on the launch of EMU, due to start on January 1, 1999.
The remaining 16 said it would have some effect.

"It may cause some turmoil in the (financial) markets. However Germany will convince the new government of the need to get public finances in order," said Peter Vanden Houte, senior economist at Bank Brussels Lambert.

Opinion polls conducted since President Jacques Chirac dissolved the National Assembly on April 21 show some gains for the socialists and their allies and in a few polls the combined support of the communists and socialists has narrowly overtaken support for the centre-right.

Analysts said possible turmoil could arise if Jospin, if he were to form the next French government, reneged on Juppe's commitment to meet a target of reducing 1997's budget deficit to three percent or less of gross domestic product (GDP).

"This would threaten France's ability to meet the deficit criteria on a sustained basis. The possibility of a delay for EMU would increase, but (that possibility) is likely to remain below 50 percent," said Michael Lewis, senior European economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.

Forecasts from 35 economists in a quarterly Reuters survey of how countries are shaping up to meet the economic criteria for EMU membership showed that France was expected comfortably to meet the debt, inflation and long-term interest rate goals.
But the median of forecasts for France's budget deficit-to-GDP ratio was 3.05 percent, missing the Maastricht Treaty target of three percent by a whisker.
But despite the perceived failure of France to meet this yardstick, all 49 contributors to the Reuters monthly poll said they expected France to be in the first EMU wave.
Some contributors said the reluctance of the Socialists to implement the harsh measures needed for a credible start to EMU may slightly increase the chances of a delay for EMU by a year.
The Socialist party says it is committed to launching EMU and the single currency in 1999 but opposes dogmatic interpretation of the Maastricht goals.

"The project may be derailed by the Socialists asking for changes in the conditions (criteria) which are not acceptable to Germany," said Claus Vastrup, economics professor at Aarhus University in Denmark.
Chances of EMU cancellation are negligible, but increase if the Socialists get together with one of the other parties, analysts said.

"Greater dependence on the Communists might also increase the chances of a cancellation, but it is only about 10 percent," said John Arrowsmith, senior research fellow at the National Institute of Economic and Social Research, UK.
